title: The Haitian Revolution

cards.h: The only successful slave revolt that created a country
cards.b:
In the 1780s, the French colony of Saint-Domingue produced more sugar and coffee than any other place on Earth. It was also a hell for about half a million enslaved people.

In 1791, they rose. Thirteen years later, they had defeated the armies of France, Spain and Britain, and founded a nation: Haiti.

Saint-Domingue had about 500,000 enslaved people, perhaps 30,000 free people of colour and a similar number of whites. Death rates were so high that planters constantly bought more captives.

When the French Revolution began in 1789, the colony fought over who was covered by 'Rights of Man'.

In August 1791 a huge uprising began in the north, said to have been launched after a ceremony at Bois Caiman (details are debated). Plantations burned. Leaders emerged, among them Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man in his late forties who had learned to read.

In 1794, France's revolutionary government abolished slavery, and Toussaint joined the French side. He ruled the island as governor. Napoleon wanted slavery back. In 1802 he sent a big army. Toussaint was seized by trickery and died in a French prison in April 1803.

Disease, especially yellow fever, killed many French soldiers. Under Jean-Jacques Dessalines, the rebels won the battle of Vertieres (November 1803).

On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared independence, the first Black republic and the first free state in Latin America. The name Haiti was a native Taino word.

France, and other countries, refused to recognise Haiti. In 1825, France demanded 150 million francs as 'compensation' for lost property, later reduced to 90 million. Haiti borrowed from French banks and paid until 1947.

Historians link this debt to Haiti's long poverty. The US only recognised Haiti in 1862.

cards.h: Is Haiti poor because it is 'cursed'?
cards.b:
Myth: Haiti's troubles come from a curse or a pact.Fact: historians point to concrete causes: the indemnity, trade embargoes, destroyed plantations, later foreign interference and political instability. Another effect: Napoleon lost Saint-Domingue and soon sold Louisiana to the US in 1803.

The revolution also terrified slave-owners across the Americas and inspired enslaved people elsewhere.

Five things to remember

  1. Haiti's revolution began in 1791.
  2. Toussaint Louverture led it, then was captured in 1802.
  3. Haiti became independent on 1 January 1804.
  4. France demanded an indemnity in 1825.
  5. The revolution inspired many.

Think about it

  • Why did powers refuse to recognise Haiti?
  • Is it fair that the freed paid the former masters?
